newsitem.title: BULGARIA: World Bank urges Bulgaria to speed up reforms.
newsitem.headline: World Bank urges Bulgaria to speed up reforms.

text.p: A senior World Bank official on Saturday urged Bulgaria to lift all price controls and speed up privatisation, pledging the bank's support as the indebted country struggles to overcome economic crisis.
World Bank team leader Kenneth Lay also told reporters the World Bank would seek support from other international lenders.

"We had discussions about ways the World Bank can intensify the work we are doing here...we can provide technical assistance to accelerate the changes that are going to take place here," Lay told reporters.
"We covered prospects for accelerating the privatisation process which will boost revenue," he added.

Speaking after meeting Prime Minister Stefan Sofianski and President Petar Stoyanov, Lay said he was impressed by their commitment to seeing Bulgaria through the hard times to come before achieving economic growth and stability.
"What we are seeing is a conviction on behalf of the government to do the right thing," said Lay who heads the South East Europe department of the World Bank.

The World Bank is prepared to help in privatisation deals which involve granting concessions like the Bulgarian Telecommunication Company, the Sofia Airport, highways, sea and river ports, said deputy prime minister Alexander Bozhkov.
"The bank can gurantee transparency and seek approporiate investors," said Bozhkov adding that the government aimed to speed up privatisation deals which were already under way.
Lay urged the government to lift price controls on all goods and services as soon as possible and said the World Bank would provide support a social safety net.
Lay said he would seek to mobilise support from the European Union to help Bulgaria overcome an acute grain shortage. A meeting is scheduled in Brussels on Monday.

Bulgaria's current grain supplies are expected to end in 20 days and the government is negotiating deals with the United States, Russia and other sources but it will need external support to pay for the grain, said Sofianski in a televised address late on Friday.
"We had extensive discussions on the grain issue because I will be going to Brussels and we want to represent very accurately the situation we are finding here," Lay said.
The World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) suspended funding for Bulgaria last year after the ruling Socialists failed to carry out planned structural reforms.

The Socialists stepped down earlier this month after 30 days of massive protests fuelled by economic hardship. They agreed to opposition demands to hold early general elections on April 19, 20 months before the end of their term.
Stoyanov, elected with opposition support, appointed an interim cabinet which inherited paralysing fuel and bread shortages, a sinking national currency and enormous debts.
Bulgaria relies on external lending for around $1 billion of debt payments due this year, a third of which is in the first quarter. An IMF negotiating mission is also due in Sofia next week.
